title: Expose an `.py_envir_solution` object
description: There is sometimes the need to access the Python solution environment to grade student's objects against ones in the solution environment. One simple example is an exercise where we want to check if a student's dataframe is correct without having them return it as the last line. The `{gradethis}` package now has an `.envir_solution` object ([see changelog](https://pkgs.rstudio.com/gradethis/news/index.html#gradethis-02129000)) and we should similar provide a `.py_envir_solution` to support that need for Python grading.

title: Setup instructions
description:
Mention that the user needs to navitage to the R folder and then the python folder for the installation. 
Maybe something like this?

Navigate to the R folder and install:
`cd R`
`make install`

If you get errors because some R packages are missing, open up RStudio and install them. 

If you are having trouble installing internal RStudio packages, like `gradethis`, then follow steps 2a to 3 [here](https://positpbc.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ACA/pages/35949281/Managing+the+Academy+R+Environment) to get your PAT set up. If you can't access the page, then contact your manager to get the correct credentials for your Github account. 

Once you have gotten `make install` to work without errors in the R folder, move to the python folder and do the same:

`cd ../python`
`make install`

title: Checking/grading functions should error for the incorrect data type
description:
We have many checking/grading functions like `py_check_index()` that currently produce an error when passed data that is not appropriate for the particular function. Example:

```r
> library(pygradethis)
> reticulate::py_run_string('import pandas as pd; import numpy as np')
> .result <- reticulate::py_eval("2", F)
> .solution <- reticulate::py_eval("pd.DataFrame({'a':[1,2,3]})")

> py_check_index()
# Error in py_get_attr_impl(x, name, silent) : 
#  AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'index'
# In addition: Warning message:
# In value[[3L]](cond) : restarting interrupted promise evaluation
```

This has forced me to add a check like this in grading code itself which should not be necessary:

```r
if (!is_DataFrame(.py_result)) {
    fail("Your result is not a DataFrame.")
}
```

title: Checking functions list/API
description:
# Description

**Problem**: We have to result check a TON of things and we need some sorta API/pattern to do checks. 

**Working solution**: We write low-level getters/checkers that help get/check different aspects of Python types, and  high-level checkers that might compose the low-level ones to do one larger check.

Here's a basic API:

## Tables

- [x] DataFrame `py_check_dataframe()`
  - [x] tests
- [x] Series `py_check_series()`
  - [x] tests
- [x] index, `py_check_index()` (`Index/MultiIndex/<>Index`)
  - [x] tests
- [x] columns `py_check_columns()` (consists of `index`)
  - [x] tests
- [x] values `py_check_values()`
  - [x] tests

(add more as needed)

How the `-check` chunk currently looks like:

````r

# simplest is to use grading functions that directly provide default feedback
```{r, py-ex-check}
gradethis::grade_this({
  # one grading function that returns fail() if any of these fail() in order:
  # - py_grade_index()
  # - py_grade_columns()
  # - py_grade_values()
  py_grade_dataframe() 
  pass("Hooray! You got the DataFrame.")
})
```

# however, you can do lower level checks
```{r, py-ex-check}
gradethis::grade_this({
  # check index
  index_problem <- py_check_index()
  if (!is.null(index_problem)) {
    fail("Wrong index!")
  }

  # check columns
  column_problem <- py_check_index()
  if (!is.null(column_problem)) {
    fail("Wrong columns!")
  }

  # check values
  values_problem <- py_check_values()
  if (!is.null(values_problem)) {
    fail("Wrong values!")
  }

  # check dataframe
  dataframe_problem <- py_check_dataframe()
  if (!is.null(dataframe_problem)) {
    fail("Wrong dataframe!")
  }

  pass("Hooray! You got the DataFrame.")
})
```
````

Grading functions:

- [x] DataFrame `py_grade_dataframe()`
  - [x] tests
- [x] Series `py_grade_series()`
  - [x] tests
- [x] index, `py_grade_index()` (`Index/MultiIndex/<>Index`)
  - [x] tests
- [x] columns `py_grade_columns()` (consists of `index`)
  - [x] tests
- [x] values `py_grade_values()`
  - [x] tests

title: A robust `get_last_value()` for Python
description:
Using `builtins._` to get the last value in Python behaves differently when we are passing objects from the `learnr` context to the `pygradethis` context. Specifically, the `builtins` approach is not working once we're in the R exercise.checker wrapper function as it still references the old last value no matter what we execute again in Python via `reticulate`. 

A better approach is to analyze the code, iteratively walk the AST, execute statements, and evaluate expressions to get the last value to grade for result checking.

title: Make use of unittest for `grade_result`
description:
When checking several conditions for `grade_result` we should do two things that make checking more maintainable:

- [x] use existing unit testing framework (this has advantage of leveraging pandas/numpy asserts as well)
- [x] custom unittest class will help in collecting all matched conditions, number of (in)correct test cases.

which requires more fields for graded result:

- [ ] add `num_correct` and `num_total`

This requires changing the graded structure to return as well a la {gradethis}:

```r
graded(
    correct = is_correct,
    message = glue_message(
      if (is_correct) glue_correct else glue_incorrect, # nolint
      .is_correct = is_correct,
      .message = NULL,
      .correct = correct,
      .incorrect = incorrect,
      .num_correct = as.character(num_correct),
      .num_total = as.character(length(conditions))
    )
  )
```
See this [test](https://github.com/rstudio-education/gradethis/blob/c84d1281cc0cac9fc6bce6d75896e2297c02f70a/tests/testthat/test_test_result_message.R#L10-L25). We'd like something like this:

```r
grade_result_strict(
  pass_if(~ .result(3) == 4),
  pass_if(~ .result(10) == 11),
  grader_args = list(),
  learnr_args = list(last_value = example_function, envir_prep = new.env()),
  glue_correct = glue_correct_no_praise
)
```

title: consider using `astunparse` for formatting
description:
The [formatters.py](./https://github.com/nischalshrestha/pygradethis/blob/master/pygradethis/formatters.py) allows us ways to customize string returned for an `ast.AST`. 

But, perhaps it's good to have a generic function use [astunparse](https://github.com/simonpercivall/astunparse) which might handle most of the "unparsing" we'd need for feedback. We can then let library user decide whether to override the unparse for particular nodes using singledispatch just as we have been doing. This will be useful at least until we can upgrade to 3.9 which contains a built-in [ast.unparse](https://docs.python.org/3.9/library/ast.html#ast.unparse).

**Rationale**: using `astunparse` does not burden us to unravel every single ast.AST node by hand reducing duplication efforts.

*Side note: we might be able to simplify formatting on manual dispatch functions by using a `map(repr, args)` for certain nodes like Call.*

```python

```

- [x] Wrong value 
- [x] Wrong calls
- [x] ~~Formal argument name matches too many provided names~~ (Python doesn't partial match names)

These ones below are caught currently but could be re-located in the message_generation module.

- [x] Bad argument names
`foo(x=1)` => `SyntaxError: foo() got an unexpected keyword argument 'x'`
- [x] Surplus Arguments 
`foo(1,2,3)` => `TypeError: foo() takes from 1 to 2 positional arguments but 3 were given`
- [x] Missing Arguments
`foo()` => `TypeError: foo() missing 1 required positional argument: 'a'`
- [x] Duplicate names
`foo(a=1, a=2)` => `SyntaxError: keyword argument repeated`

description:

Solution expects: `1 + sum([1,2])`

"I did not expect 3 in `sum([1,2,3])`"

or more specifically:

"I did not expect 3 in `[1,2,3]`"

title: call standardization for function checking
description:
For a function call, students may supply some arguments or only some specify keywords. We want to standardize the call.

For e.g.:

Student: `df.head(10)`
Solution: `df.head(n=10)`

We want to first standardize the student's function call to be `df.head(n=10)` before checking against solution.

Tasks:

- [x] inspect ast.Call(s) and be able standardize arguments to formal parameters (setting defaults etc.)
- [x] be able to check whether user vs solution calls are the same or not
- [x] ensure that these checks play nice with expressions that include calls
